Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
For sixteen years, Omar had run toward danger. As a firefighter, his identity was built on being the one who stayed calm when others panicked, the one who could be counted on in the worst moments. That sense of self began to crumble over three months last spring. It started subtly: a man on a bicycle who seemed to be on his street every time he left for a shift, then at the grocery store, then circling the park where he walked his dog. The feeling of being watched intensified until the day the man confronted him at the end of his own driveway, muttering threats Omar couldn't quite decipher but whose malice was unmistakable. After a restraining order and a tense month, the man was gone, but the sense of being hunted remained lodged deep in Omar's mind.

In the weeks that followed, the world became a minefield of reminders. Seeing a bicycle chained to a post could instantly bring the memory rushing back, not as a coherent story but as a series of sharp, overwhelming fragments: the glint of sun on the handlebars, the low, menacing voice, the sudden, paralyzing fear. When the memory returned, he felt so swamped by emotion that he had to brace himself against a wall, fighting for breath. Because the intrusions were so visceral and unpredictable, he found himself constantly scanning his environment for anything that might set one off, becoming hyper-aware of every bicycle or person who seemed out of place. He knew what had happened, but when his wife asked, he found he was unable to find the words to describe the suffocating helplessness of it. The memory itself was a constant source of threat; reliving the confrontation made the quiet suburban street outside his window feel acutely dangerous, and he began checking the locks on the doors three, four times before bed, convinced the threat was not in the past but simply waiting.

The intrusions were not just frightening; they felt like a personal failing. Each time the memory broke through, it served as proof of his own inadequacy. He was a firefighter, trained to handle threats, yet he had been powerless and terrified. This dissonance solidified into a harsh self-judgment: he was a weak person. This belief began to colour everything. The simple act of feeling someone walking too close behind him on the sidewalk would send a jolt of panic through him, followed immediately by a hot wave of shame. What kind of man is scared of his own shadow? he would think, the self-recrimination confirming his weakness all over again.

This conviction that he was fundamentally changed for the worse, that some essential strength in him had been broken, fueled a state of constant, exhausting vigilance. Because he had come to believe he was weak, he felt he had to be perpetually on guard against a world that now seemed filled with hidden dangers. At the firehouse, a place that had once been a second home, he found himself scanning for exits the moment he walked into the kitchen. He watched the other firefighters, men he had trusted with his life for years, with a new and unnerving suspicion, scrutinizing their expressions for any sign of aggression. He was on high alert for any unexpected sound-a dropped tool, a car backfiring on the street-each noise a potential attack he needed to be ready for.

This relentless hypervigilance only served to tighten the loop. The sheer exhaustion of scanning, watching, and jumping at shadows became, in his mind, further evidence that he was losing control. This isn't normal, he concluded. My reactions mean I'm going crazy. This fear of his own mind collapsing made him try to force the memory into submission, to replay the events over and over, searching for the key to what was wrong with him. But this only brought back the overwhelming feelings with more intensity. His fear of going crazy also made him exquisitely sensitive to his triggers; because he believed himself to be so fragile, he became hyper-aware of every bicycle, every person who lingered too long in his line of sight, which in turn brought the memory crashing back more frequently.

His world had shrunk. He stopped going to the park and started taking a longer, convoluted route to the station to avoid the street where the man had confronted him. His wife noticed his distance, the way he would flinch if she came up behind him too quietly. The breaking point came during a routine call-a small kitchen fire-when the sound of a smoke alarm, a noise he'd heard a thousand times, sent such a wave of panic through him that he froze for a full three seconds. No one else noticed, but he did. He came to therapy a week later, his voice low as he admitted his deepest fear: that he was no longer the man his wife married, no longer the firefighter his team could rely on, and that this broken, terrified version of himself was all he would ever be.
